# Scale benchmark (generated by `python -m pipeline.bench`)

1000 tickets arriving at once, worked by 3 sessions in parallel (one schema each, like separate banks), against 4,487,133 AMLworld transactions. Ran 2026-10-28 22:53:57 on Windows 11, AMD64, 16 logical CPUs, Python 3.14.3; Exasol 2026.2.0-nano.3.

## The golden hour

**1000 of 1000 tickets were worked within an hour of all arriving together.** Median time to hold 16.7 min, 95th percentile 32.7 min, last ticket 34.3 min. 29.2 tickets a minute.

One ticket's own work: median 5.76 s, 95th percentile 7.14 s, slowest 1.9 min.

## Time per step

| Step | Median | 95th percentile | Slowest |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| intake | 0.40 s | 0.54 s | 0.98 s |
| trace | 0.63 s | 0.85 s | 1.38 s |
| attribute | 1.14 s | 1.49 s | 2.20 s |
| score | 2.06 s | 2.56 s | 3.27 s |
| rules | 0.71 s | 0.97 s | 1.18 s |
| checks | 0.41 s | 0.55 s | 1.01 s |
| holds | 0.37 s | 0.53 s | 1.8 min |

## What happened to the tickets

- Worked to the end: 1000; with at least one hold: 956 (Rs 79,034,554,927 held in all).
- Intake found no exact match (nothing held, as at a bank): 0.
- Checks failed (nothing held automatically): 0.
- Stopped by an error: 0.

Each complaint reaches the bank 30 minutes after the payment, so the trace follows what had moved by then; money that moves later is the watch's job, as at a bank. Every ticket counts as arriving at the same moment, so the time to hold includes the wait in the queue: the worst case of a night when many complaints land together. In the lab schemas one bank owns every AMLworld account, so each trace follows every hop: more work than a bank that sees only its own. A laptop, not a bank's servers: the numbers are a floor to improve on, not a promise.
